opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually. For a long time, part of the motivation for studying mathematics was almost instrumental: you learn it because it's hard, because it's a gateway to physics, engineering, finance, computer science. Mathematical skill was a scarce resource, and scarcity gives you a sense of purpose. You feel needed.

AI shakes that up. When a model can solve competition problems, help formalize proofs, or check a long computation in seconds, the "I'm doing this because no one else can" justification gets weaker. I've talked to students who feel a kind of quiet anxiety about that: if a machine can do the exercise, why am I struggling with it for three hours?

But I think that framing confuses the exercise with the point. When you struggle with a problem, the output isn't really the answer. The output is a change in you: how you see structure, how you hold several ideas in your head at once, how you tell the difference between something that feels true and something that is true. AI doesn't take that away from you. It can only take it away if you let it do the struggling on your behalf.

So I'd say the sense of purpose shifts in a few ways. First, it moves from producing answers to understanding and judgment. Someone still has to decide which questions matter, which definitions are natural, and whether a result actually means what we think it means. That is deeply human work, and it becomes more important, not less, when the cost of generating proofs drops.

Second, mathematics becomes a bit more like music or chess. Engines play chess far better than any human, and yet more people play chess today than ever before. People don't play because they're the best in the world; they play because the activity itself is beautiful and it trains the mind. I think mathematics can be loved in the same way, for its own sake.

And third, honestly, AI can make mathematics more accessible. A student in a small town without a great teacher can now have something like a patient tutor that explains an idea five different ways. That could bring many more people into the subject.

So my view is: AI removes some of the external reasons to study mathematics, but it clarifies the internal ones. If your purpose was to be a calculator, that purpose is gone. If your purpose is to understand, it has never been more alive.

r001.rationale: The response says AI weakens the idea that mathematical skill is scarce and needed, but it does not describe a narrowed path from studying mathematics to making a meaningful contribution through a mathematical career.

r002.rationale: It discusses instrumental reasons for studying mathematics, but does not say that students are shifting toward studying it for university admission.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've been sitting with a lot lately, honestly. When I started studying math, the sense of purpose was quite simple. There were problems nobody had solved, and if I worked hard enough, maybe I could be the one to solve them. That was the whole motivation. It was personal. Now you have systems that can produce proofs for competition problems, that can check arguments faster than any human referee, and increasingly they can suggest directions I wouldn't have thought of. So the naive version of purpose, "I'm the one who will find this," gets shaken.

But I don't think purpose disappears. I think it shifts. Let me say what I mean. First, a lot of what mathematicians do was never really about producing the final theorem. It's about understanding. A proof that a machine generates and I can't follow doesn't give me understanding, it gives me a certificate. And for most of us, the reason we got into this was the feeling of suddenly seeing why something is true. That feeling isn't taken away by AI. If anything, AI makes it more available, because you can ask it to explain, to try a special case, to show you where the argument breaks.

Second, I think the role of taste becomes much more important. Deciding which questions matter, which definitions are the right ones, which directions are worth years of someone's life. Machines are getting good at answering, but choosing what to ask is still deeply human, at least for now. In the past, taste was something you developed slowly, almost as a side effect of doing calculations for ten years. Now I think it becomes the main thing.

And third, maybe this is more emotional than intellectual, but I'll say it. Studying mathematics was never purely instrumental. People learn to play the piano even though recordings exist. People climb mountains even though helicopters exist. There's a version of purpose that's about becoming a certain kind of person, someone who can think clearly, hold a difficult structure in their head, tolerate being confused for a long time. AI doesn't do that for you. You still have to go through it.

So for students who ask me, "Why should I study math if AI can do it," my honest answer is that the purpose was never "because nobody else can." It was "because this is how you learn to see." I do think the field will change a lot, and some careers that existed before won't exist in the same form. I'd be lying if I said that doesn't worry me. But the core reason to study it, I think, is still intact.

r001.rationale: The response says AI shakes the motivation of being the person to solve a problem and may change some careers, but it does not clearly describe a narrowed path from studying mathematics to making a meaningful contribution through a mathematical career.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe studying mathematics for university admission rather than for the subject itself.

astra-6.text:
I think AI pushes us to distinguish between getting an answer and understanding something. If the purpose of studying mathematics is only to solve a prescribed problem as quickly as possible, then AI can make that purpose feel less convincing. But getting an answer was never the whole point.

When you study mathematics, you learn to ask what follows from an assumption, where an argument breaks, and whether two apparently different problems share the same structure. Even if AI gives you a proof, there’s still a difference between reading it and understanding why the key idea works—and when you might use it elsewhere.

So I don’t think the purpose disappears. The emphasis shifts toward judgment: choosing questions, recognizing useful ideas, and deciding what deserves our confidence. And there’s still a very personal pleasure in understanding something that used to confuse you. Having a machine that can do it doesn’t take that experience away.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI pushes us to ask what studying mathematics is really for. If the purpose is simply to get an answer, then having a machine that can do much of the calculation can make that purpose feel less compelling. But getting an answer and understanding why it is true are different things.

For me, the purpose shifts toward learning how to ask good questions, recognize structure, and judge whether an argument makes sense. AI can suggest a solution, but you still need enough mathematical understanding to examine its assumptions and catch a convincing mistake.

And there is still the pleasure of understanding something yourself. Even if a tool can produce a proof immediately, working through the idea can change how you think. So I would hope AI makes mathematics less about competing at calculation and gives more people a way into that experience of discovery.
